title: Navigate the Claude Ecosystem
summary: Choose deliberately among Claude's conversational workspace, developer platform, API, and coding-agent surfaces without confusing their controls or operating models.
objectives: Distinguish interactive Claude workspaces from API-integrated and coding-agent workflows.
Select a Claude surface from user, control, data, automation, and operational requirements.
Verify volatile product capabilities against current Anthropic sources before promising them.
Document the identity, credential, data, tool, and review boundaries for a Claude workflow.

sections.title: One ecosystem has different operating surfaces
paragraphs: Claude can support direct knowledge work in a conversational product, reusable project workspaces with instructions and knowledge, application integrations through the Claude API, and repository work through coding-agent tools. These surfaces may share model capabilities, but they do not share the same user experience, authentication, billing, data controls, tools, or deployment responsibilities.

Begin with the job rather than a model name. An individual drafting from supplied documents needs a different operating boundary from a production application serving many users or an agent authorized to edit a repository.
sections.callout: A provider is not a single product surface. Name the surface whenever you describe a capability or control.

code.label: One ecosystem has different operating surfaces (Code Implementation)

sections.title: Match the surface to the work
paragraphs: Use a conversational workspace for supervised exploration, drafting, analysis, and reusable project context. Use the API when software must provide inputs, enforce contracts, select tools, validate outputs, observe failures, or serve a repeatable workflow. Use a coding-agent surface when the task requires repository context, commands, file changes, tests, and source-control evidence.

The same task can move between surfaces. A person might explore the requirement in Claude, prototype an instruction in the Console, integrate it through the API, and later delegate bounded repository work to a coding agent. Record what changes at each transition.

code.label: Match the surface to the work (Code Implementation)

sections.title: Controls follow the surface
paragraphs: For every workflow, identify the acting user or service, credential type, data source, retention arrangement, available tools, permission boundary, budget, logs, and required human review. Do not infer API data handling from a consumer product setting or assume that an interactive feature exists in an API.

Keep API secrets outside prompts, examples, repositories, and learning evidence. Applications should load credentials from their runtime environment or a managed secret store, scope access to the workload, and rotate or revoke credentials through an operational process.

code.label: Claude surface decision record
code.code:
outcome: [USER-VISIBLE RESULT]
surface: [CLAUDE WORKSPACE | CONSOLE | API | CODING AGENT]
actor: [PERSON OR SERVICE]
identityAndCredential: [CONTROLLED REFERENCE, NEVER SECRET VALUE]
trustedData: [SOURCES + CLASSIFICATION]
toolsAndPermissions: [ALLOWLIST + LIMITS]
validation: [OUTPUT + POSTCONDITION CHECKS]
humanReview: [WHEN + BY WHOM]
currentSource: [OFFICIAL URL + VERIFIED DATE]

sections.title: Separate stable concepts from volatile facts
paragraphs: The need to authenticate, define data boundaries, validate results, and observe a production workflow is stable. Product names, model identifiers, limits, pricing, plan eligibility, supported regions, and feature availability are volatile.

Teach stable decision patterns in the lesson and link volatile details to the current official page with a verification date. Before procurement, release, or user-facing commitments, recheck the official source in the relevant account, plan, region, and deployment environment.

code.label: Separate stable concepts from volatile facts (Code Implementation)

sections.title: Build a surface map before implementation
paragraphs: A useful surface map connects each user journey to its Claude interface, identity, input sources, output consumer, tools, approvals, evidence, and failure owner. It also names what the workflow does not do.

Review the map with product, security, data, and operations stakeholders. If a requirement depends on a plan-specific or newly released capability, attach the official evidence and a revalidation date rather than relying on memory.

code.label: Build a surface map before implementation (Code Implementation)

activity.title: Design a Claude surface map
instructions: Choose one realistic workflow and write its user, outcome, inputs, sensitivity, frequency, integration needs, and consequence of failure.
Compare a conversational workspace, the Claude API, and a coding-agent surface against those requirements; mark unsupported or unverified assumptions.
Select one surface and complete the identity, credential, data, tool, validation, logging, review, and failure-owner fields.
Attach at least two current official Anthropic sources and record the verification date for each volatile claim.
evidence: A three-surface comparison with a justified selection and explicit rejected alternatives.
A completed control map that contains no credential value and links every volatile capability claim to dated official evidence.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which requirement changed your choice of surface, and which fact must be rechecked before implementation?

cues.text: Treat Claude as an ecosystem of conversational, developer, API, and coding-agent surfaces with different controls and responsibilities.
Choose the operating surface from the user journey, automation, integration, supervision, and evidence the work requires.
Map identity, credentials, data, tools, permissions, validation, logs, budgets, and human review for the selected surface.
Keep stable operating principles in the lesson and verify changing models, limits, plans, regions, pricing, and features at the official source.
Turn the selection into a reviewable surface map that names owners, evidence, exclusions, and every assumption that can expire.
Place workspace, API, and coding-agent options beside columns for user, control, automation, data, tools, and operations.
cues.accessibilityAlternative: A static comparison table lists workspace, API, and coding-agent rows against user, control, automation, data, tools, and operations columns.

cues.text: Ask learners which control is lost when a supervised chat prototype becomes an unattended application.
Allow two minutes to label three requirements as stable principles or volatile product facts.
Check that the selected surface is justified and every volatile assumption has official evidence and a verification date.
Guide the learner through the comparison, selection, control map, and source verification.
Begin the check after the learner can distinguish surfaces without transferring controls or capabilities between them.

questions.prompt: What should determine the choice between a Claude workspace, API, and coding-agent surface?
choices: The newest model name
The required user journey, controls, integration, supervision, and evidence
One permanent default for every workflow
The longest available context window
questions.explanation: The operating requirements determine the surface; a model name or one capability cannot represent the complete workflow.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly handles product data controls?
choices: A consumer setting automatically applies to every API deployment
All Claude surfaces have identical retention behavior
Verify the data arrangement for the exact product surface and deployment
Data controls can be inferred from the model family
questions.explanation: Controls differ by product and deployment arrangement and must be verified for the actual surface.

questions.prompt: Where should an application keep its Claude API credential?
choices: In a runtime environment or managed secret store
Inside the prompt template
In a committed example file
In learner evidence
questions.explanation: Credentials belong in an operational secret boundary, never in prompts, repositories, examples, or evidence.

questions.prompt: Which item is most likely to require frequent official-source revalidation?
choices: The need to authenticate an API
The need to validate consequential output
The principle of least privilege
A current plan's feature eligibility and limits
questions.explanation: Plan eligibility, limits, prices, regions, features, and model identifiers are volatile product facts.

questions.prompt: What makes a Claude surface map implementation-ready?
choices: It lists only the preferred model
It records identity, data, tools, permissions, validation, review, evidence, exclusions, and failure ownership
It assumes the prototype's controls will transfer
It avoids naming unsupported requirements
questions.explanation: An implementation-ready map identifies the workflow boundaries, evidence, and owners needed to operate the selected surface.
